3. The facts of the case, in short, are that the respondents other lands had earlier been acquired by the Government for the purpose of construction of Dhaka-Chittagong Highway and thereafter only the case plots are left to them and they want to develop the same for the purpose of setting up industry on these lands. If the lands in the case plots are acquired they will have no means of livelihood and will be thrown to the street as landless people. It is further asserted that the writ-respondent No.5 has 3.49 acres of land on the other side of Dhaka-Chittagong Road near the case land but the writ-respondent No.5 instead of setting up the industry on his own land managed to get the said property acquired by influencing local administration to grab the properties of the petitioners at a low cost. It is further asserted that although it is shown in paper that the case plots have been acquired by the Government and possession of the same has been handed over to the requiring body but, in fact, the petitioners are still in possession of the respective case plots and it was never taken over by the respondent No.5. It is further contended that the acquisition case has been started with malafide intention as the writ-respondent No. 5 could set up his industry on his own land which is sufficient for establishing the industry in question. It is further alleged that even after acquisition of the case land the writ-respondent No. 5 is not utilising the same for over the long 9 years and, as such, the acquisition order is liable to be struck down on this count as well. 

 4. The writ-respondent No. 5 contested the writ petition contending, inter alia, that the land in question was acquired under Ordinance No. 2 of 1982 for setting up an industry which is for public purpose. It has further asserted that according to the provisions of the Ordinance, objection was filed in response to the notice served under section 3 of the Ordinance and the same was heard and thereafter, the report was sent to the Divisional Commissioner who rejected the objection and duty accorded his approval. The publication of the Gazette Notification was made on 31-12-1992 vesting the land in the Government and the Government thereafter handed over vacant possession of the case land to the requiring body and they are in possession of the same since 31-12-1991. It is also asserted that an agreement has been concluded on 14-8-1990 in accordance with section 15 of the Ordinance. It appears that the Ministry of Land by its memo dated 4-9-1990 asked the Deputy Commissioner to take necessary steps to acquire at least 2.50 acres of land by LA Case No. 60 of 1987-88 or any other land for Mullah Industrial Estate and subsequently LA Case No.1 of 1990-91 was started. Thus, the case property was acquired for the writ-respondent No.5 in accordance with law. The added writ-respondent No. 5 also filed an affidavit-in-opposition wherein they denied the material allegations made in the writ petition and contended, inter alia, that as per recommendation of the Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Land and the District Land Allotment Committee, Comilla, started LA Case No.1 of 1990-91 after complying with all the procedures as per law. The case land has been acquired for setting up an export oriented industry and transferred the acquired land to the writ-respondent No.5. It is asserted that the land has been acquired for the purpose of public interest and public purpose and the writ-respondent No.5 requires an area of 2.50 acres of land and writ- respondent No.5 has already set up the said industry for producing tooth brush-D-sticks, staple pins, gem clips, educational toys, etc. and the possession of the land has duly been handed over to writ-respondent No. 5 whereupon a portion of the land has been developed and structures raised thereon for running the industry. It further appears that this writ- respondent filed title suit No. 72 of 1996 on 28-5- 1996 against the writ-petitioners of Writ Petition No. 5392 of 1996 for permanent injunction in the Court of Assistant Judge, Daudkandi, Comilla over the selfsame property and an order for maintaining status quo was passed on 28-5-1998 in respect of the suit land and the proceeding of the suit has been stayed. 

 5. Leave was granted to consider the submission of the learned Counsel for the appellant that "the petitioners took the selfsame grounds before us to assail the order of the High Court Division. They have urged that the acquisition was for public purpose and that the High Court Division erred in law in finding it malafide, inasmuch as the requiring body had allegedly had some land near the acquired land. They have also urged that the High Court Division erred in finding that the acquisition was made at the behest of the Ministry of Land and the High Court Division failed to notice that the writ petition was an inordinate belated one." 

 6. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant, submitted that the acquisition is for public purpose and in public interest; that the High Court Division erred in finding malafide only because the petitioner allegedly had some land nearby the acquired land and the acquisition proceeding had been started on the order passed by the Ministry of Land; that no malice of the Government or officials against the writ-petitioner having been alleged or established by adequate materials, the High Court Division erred in holding the acquisition proceeding to be malafide. The learned Advocate further submitted that the High Court Division erred in exercising inordinate delay in challenging the acquisition, ignoring that a vested right had accrued to the appellant having acted bonafide on such acquisition for long time. Furthermore, the learned Advocate submits that the acquisition has been made in accordance with the law and not at the behest of any other inasmuch as the writ petition was filed as a measure of afterthought long after the industry has already been set up. 

 7. Mr Faruque Ahmed, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondent, submitted that the High Court Division has committed no wrong in making the Rule absolute declaring that requisition has been initiated and started without any lawful authority; that the proceeding of Land Acquisition Case No. 1 of 1990-91 at the office of the respondent No.4, insofar it relates to the acquisition of the property of the writ-petitioners of Mouza Uzar Bhanga JL No. 165, Police Station Daudkandi, District-Comilla appertaining to RS Khatian No. 202 Plot No. 380 measuring 0.7 acre out of 0.14 acre of land as evidenced by Annexure-C, the writ petition is required to be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 11. It has been alleged by the respondent that no notice under section 7 was served in respect of Plot No. 342 and the writ-petitioners had not received any compensation in respect of the case land but the law provides that the notification has to spell out whether the land is acquired on the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner or Divisional Commissioner or the Government as the case may be and in the present case though it has been mentioned that on the satisfaction of the Government the land has been acquired but the Divisional Commissioner has accorded final approval to the acquisition proposal. 

 13. Upon notice under section 3 dated 2-7-1990 an objection was filed on 15-7-1990 Annexure-D. The appellant did not state about his possession of any land in the vicinity of the acquired land. The respondents accordingly filed a representation to the Ministry alleging that the appellant has 3.49 acres of land in the vicinity of the acquired land. 

 15. In view of the specific mention about the plots and area of the land owned by the appellant which could be utilised for the purpose instead of acquiring the land, I do not find any reason whatsoever for the appellant to go for acquisition of land in the vicinity for setting up an alleged export oriented industry leaving aside his own land in the vicinity totaling an area of 3.49 acres of land on the side of Dhaka-Chittagong Highway and this aspect of the case was overlooked by the District Land Allotment Committee in deciding the allotment of the land in favour of appellant through LA Case No. 1 of 1990- 91. The respondents herein have also brought to the notice of the said fact by Annexure-H in the writ- petition to the authority concerned but the authority gave a deaf ear to the said representation. It appears from the submission of the learned Assistant Attorney-General before the High Court Division that though it is apparent from the record that the notices were duly served on some persons but the real owner of Plot No. 342 of the case land has not admittedly been served with the notices of acquisition of the suit land. Thus, the said non-service of notices for acquisition vitiated the acquisition proceedings itself. 

 18. It may be noted that no notice under section 7 was ever served in respect of Plot No. 342 and the respondent had not received any compensation in respect of the said case land. Although it has been clearly provided by law that the notification must contain the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner or Divisional Commissioner or the Government as the requirement of the acquired land, but in the instant notice it appears that the Authority has simply given a mechanical nod regarding acquisition without applying its mind on the facts and circumstances of the case. The infirmity in the notice could not be remedied or corrected even though the gazette notification for acquisition of the land has been effected giving alleged validity of the acquisition. Thus it appears from the record that the non- issuance of the mandatory notice under the provision of the Ordinance No. II of 1982 has vitiated the acquisition proceeding and in that view of the matter, illegal publication of gazette could not be a sufficient ground for covering any defect in the acquisition proceedings. 

 20. As to the assertion of the writ-petitioner that the appellant possesses 3.49 acres of land on the other side of the road which has been not denied by making any statement in the affidavit-in-opposition except by way of a general, vague and evasive reply and without even denying specifically that the said plots do not belong to him or that he has no right, title and interest in those plots. This aspect of the respondent's case has not been considered by the Authority or the Land Allotment Committee. But contrary to the provision of Article 29(2)(d) of the Requisition and Acquisition of Property Act, 1982 which cast duty upon the authority to see even if it is possible for the requiring body to set up the industry on its own land measuring 3.49 acres of land in proximity of the acquired land, the appellant had acquired 2.50 acres of land belonging to the respondents. Furthermore, no attempt was ever taken by the appellant to approach the respondent for purchase of the land in question and there is nothing on the record to show why these particular plots of land have been found suitable for the said industry. 

 21. The High Court Division has detailed the circumstances and the speed by which the acquisition proceeding was undertaken and completed. It is apparent from a Government Memo dated 9-4-1990 whereby the Deputy Commissioner, Comilia was asked to take necessary steps to acquire at least 2.50 acres of land in LA Case No. 65 of 1987-88 or any other land for the appellant. Thereafter, the appellant filed an application on 3-6-1990 for acquiring 2.50 acres of land and the allotment committee soon thereafter on 21-6-1990 approved the proposal by initiating LA Case No.1 of 1990-91. The proceeding at such hot haste clearly shows the speed and the motive behind acquisition of the land and completing the entire drama of acquisition within such unusual and short period. 

 22. These circumstances manifest the non- application of the mind of the District Allotment Committee and the acquiring authority in the matter of acquisition of the land in question for the appellant. 

 23. The High Court Division also took note of the malafide in the matter of initiating and conducting the requisition proceeding and on the principle that malafide vitiated everything declared the acquisition proceeding illegal and without any jurisdiction. 

 24. It is important for the authority concerned to arrive at a finding that the acquisition is expedient for a public purpose or public interest and to cause a public notice to be given for acquisition and requisition of the property but as it could be gathered from the circumstances and speed, the proceeding was undertaken and disposed of by the authority giving deaf ear to the stages of proceeding of the acquisition of property pursuant to the provisions of the Act. It is also a glaring example of evading the process of law by directing Deputy Commission to take necessary steps for acquiring 3.49 in LA Case No. 65 of 1987-88 or any other case for the petitioner on 9-4-1990 and soon thereafter completing acquisition proceeding in such a hot haste initiating afresh the LA Case No.1 of 1990-91 after the said alleged proposal incidentally on LA Case No. 65 of 1987-88. 

 28. The respondents, as writ petitioners, filed Writ Petition Nos. 5392 of 1996 and 576 of 1198 challenging the proceeding of Land Acquisition Case No.1 of 1990-91, insofar it relates to the acquisition of property of the writ petitioners of Mouza Ozar Bhanga, JL No.165, Police Station-Daudkandi, Cornilla comprising 2.50 acres of Plot Nos. 342 and 381 being the subject matter of Writ Petition No. 5392 of 1976 and Plot No. 380 being the subject matter of Writ Petition No. 576 of 1998 hereinafter called the case land as without lawful authority and for a direction on the writ-respondent appellants to drop the said proceeding. 

 29. The common case of the writ petitioners is that the Government has already acquired their other lands for the construction of Dhaka-Chittagong Highway and they are only left with the case land which they wanted to develop for the purpose of setting up their own industry. If the case land is acquired they will be thrown out on to the street. The writ respondent No. 5, M/s Mollah Industrial Estate, on the other hand, has 3.49 acres of land in the vicinity of the case land on the other side of Dhaka- Chittagong Highway. Despite this, the writ-respondent No. 5, without setting up its aforesaid industry on its own land managed the case land to be acquired for setting up its industry by influencing the local administration. Although the case land is shown in paper to have been acquired by the Government and possession handed over to writ- respondent No.5 as the requiring body but, in fact, the writ petitioners are still in possession of the case land and the same are not taken over and utilised by the writ-respondent No. 5. It is also stated that the acquisition of the case land is malafide as the same is caused to have been acquisitioned by the Government for the purpose of setting up of the industry of the writ-respondent No.5, although writ respondent has its own land across the Dhaka-Chittagong Highway within the vicinity of the case land. 

 30. The writ-respondent No. 5 contested the Rule issued in both the writ petitions, contending that the case land was acquired by the Government to enable the writ-respondent No. 5 to set up their export-oriented industry, which was for public purpose, by issuing notice under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 inviting objections from all the concerned, including the writ-petitioners and the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla, after due hearing of the objections, submitted the record of the proceedings with his opinion to the Divisional Commissioner for his decision. The Divisional Com- missioner, thereafter, on consideration of the said report of the Deputy Commissioner, made a decision for acquisition of the case land and the Deputy Commissioner then issued a public notice under section 6 inviting claims for compensation informing all the concerned that the Divisional Commissioner took a decision to acquire the case land and would take possession of the same followed by a notice under section 7 for awarding compensation. All the concerned received payment of compensation except the writ-petitioners, who purposely refused to take compensation. Subsequently Gazette notification under section 11 of the Ordinance was published on 31-12-1992 vesting the case land on the Government and thereafter the possession thereof was handed over to the writ- respondent No. 5 i.e. the requiring body on 31-12- 1991. 

 31. The High Court Division, thereafter, on hearing the parties made the Rules absolute on the grounds that the acquisition of the case land is not for public purpose. The case land insofar as it belonged to the writ-petitioners has not been utilised by the requiring body i.e. the writ respondent No.5 and the same is still in possession of the writ-petitioners and that the acquisition is malafide, inasmuch as the case land is managed to have been acquired leaving aside 3.49 acres of land of the writ- respondent No. 5 in the vicinity. Accordingly, the delay in filing the writ-petitions under reference shall not prejudicially affect the right of the writ- petitioners to have the case land dropped from the said LA Case No. 1/90-91. 

 32. Against this backdrop, leave was granted to consider whether the acquisition in question is for public purpose, whether the acquisition of the case land is malafide for procuring acquisition of the case land leaving aside the land of the writ-respondent No. 5 situated in the vicinity on whether the delay in filing the aforesaid two writ-petitions by the writ- petitioners was inordinate and fatal for both the acquiring and the requiring body and thus rendering the writ petitions as not maintainable. 

 34. It is noted from the record that the writ respondent No. 5, Mollah Industrial Estate, as the requiring body, approached the Government and made a proposal for acquisition of land for them to the extent of 2.50 acres at the present site to enable them to set up export-oriented industry and entered into an agreement dated 14-2-1990, in this regard with the Government under section 15 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982. Consequently, the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla published a notice under section 3, proposing to acquire lands mentioned, therein including the case land for public purpose to enable the writ-respondent No. 5 to set up an export- oriented industry inviting objections from the affected persons against such acquisition. The writ- petitioners filed objection on 15-7-1990 to the Deputy Commissioner. The Deputy Commissioner thereafter on due hearing of the objections submitted the record of the proceedings held by him to the Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong along with his report for his decision. The Divisional Commissioner thereupon on due consideration of the report together with the objections of the writ- petitioners gave his decision in favour of acquisition of the said land as contemplated under section 5 of the said Ordinance after rejecting the objections. The Deputy Commissioner thereafter issued a public notice under section 6 dated 2-3-1991 intimating the said decision of the Divisional Commissioner, inviting claims for compensation from all the concerned including the writ petitioners. 

 35. The writ-petitioners, in response thereto, submitted their objection dated 22-10-1991 to the Ministry of Land pointing out for the first time that the writ-respondent No. 5 had their own land measuring 3.49 acres across the Dhaka-Chittagong Highway which is close to the acquired land, with a request not to acquire their land. Their objection was rejected on due enquiry. The writ-respondent No.5 thereupon deposited compensation money to the Government, as per the estimate furnished by the Government and thereafter the Deputy Commissioner arranged for payment of compensation to the affected. All the concerned received the compensation money for their land but the writ-petitioners refused to receive compensation for the case land. Accordingly, the compensation money has been kept in the public account of the Republic. The case land, consequently, finally stood acquired and vested in the Government and the Government there- after handed over possession of the same to the writ-respondent No.5 on 2-12-1991 and the Deputy Commissioner then published a declaration of the acquisition of the case land and other land in the official Gazette on 31-12-1992. The writ-petitioners then filed Writ Petition No. 5392 of 1996 after 2 years and Writ Petition No. 576 of 1998 after 7 years of the final vesting of the case land to the Government on publication of the said official Gazette. 

 36. A property is said to be needed for public purpose or in the public interest when it is acquisitioned in furtherance of the general interest of the community as opposed to the particular interest of the individuals. When the Divisional Commissioner makes a decision for acquisition of a property under section 5(1) of the Ordinance such decision is conclusive evidence that the property is needed for public purpose or in the public interest. In this view of the legal position and when it could not be established by the writ-petitioners that payment of compensation was withheld by the Government after the decision of acquisition of the case land was made or taken by the Divisional Commissioner the proceedings of the said LA Case No.1 of 1990-91 shall not abate. The case of Alauddin Khandker vs Secretary, Ministry of Land, 4 BLC (AD) 25 may be profitably referred to in this regard. 

 37. Since in the present case, the case land was finally vested in the Government on publication of the official Gazette under section 11, the filing of the said two writ-petitions challenging the acquisition proceeding in question was abortive, ineffectual and meaningless, inasmuch as such inordinate delay in filing the writ-petitions disentitled the writ-petitioners relief sought for. In fact, the writ-Court erred in entertaining such delayed writ-petitions, inasmuch as the rights which accrued to the Government and the writ-respondent No.5 by reason of such delay were not liable to be disturbed and interfered with; case of Bangladesh vs Golam Azam 46 DLR (AD) 192 can be cited on the point. 

 38. Now the only pertinent question that falls for consideration is, whether the acquisition under consideration is malafide. The answer to this question depends on whether the case land was acquisitioned despite the fact that the writ-respondent No.5 has sufficient quantum of land in the neighbourhood of the case land. It is already noticed that the writ-petitioners did not make this allegation in their written objection to the notices issued under section 3 as well as under section 6 by the Deputy Commissioner. They only made a belated objection on 22-10-1991 in this regard to the Ministry of Land, much after the decision was taken by the Divisional Commissioner for acquisition of the case land. Moreover, the writ-petitioners could not establish the allegation about the existence of any land of the writ-respondent No. 5 in or about the vicinity of the acquired land by producing any authentic or official document when the writ-respondent No. 5 denied the same. It is therefore, clear that the allegation of the malafide acquisition stands disproved. On the other hand, in the face of denial of this allegation by the writ-respondent No.5 the writ-petitions under reference could be said to have involved disputed question of fact making the writ-petitions not maintainable. 

 39. It is already noticed that the acquisition proceeding in the present case already reached its finality with the case land vested in the Government long before the said writ petitions were filed. Now even after this if the writ-respondent No. 5 is allegedly found to have failed to utilise or use the case land for the purpose it was acquired, the Court cannot provide any relief by way of restoration of possession of the case land to the writ-petitioners by setting aside the acquisition proceeding which acquisition was long complete and legally made. When any land is otherwise validly acquisitioned such acquisition cannot be interfered with, except on the ground that the acquisition was malafide and/or compensation for the land was not paid. No such case has been made out by the writ-petitioners. In a case where it is established that the requiring body has failed to use or utilise the acquired land for the purpose it was acquired the Government can make the requiring body surrender such land to the Deputy Commissioner and, in that case, on the application made by the real owners of the land, the Government in its discretion may restore possession of such land to them.
